extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy and the history of morals
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria and explanatory standards used to assess moral beliefs, pleasures, and duties across societies; focuses on distinctions (higher/lower pleasures, duties of conscience vs positive commands), causes of moral variation, and the role of education, custom, and dogma. Useful for analyzing historical and philosophical accounts of moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of higher and lower pleasures (quality as well as quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This distinction of kind has been neglected or denied by most utilitarian writers... If the reality of the distinction be admitted, it shows that our wills are so far from tending necessarily to that which produces most enjoyment that we have the power even in our pleasures of recognising a higher and a wholly different quality..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: Farce often gives more unmingled and intense pleasure than tragedy, yet tragedy's pleasure is 'of a higher order.' Music elevates, eating lowers; beauty produces a mixed melancholy, grotesque produces more violent pleasure. If pleasures differ in kind as well as quantity, choices can be made for 'worthiness' rather than sheer enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilisation raises the standard and elaboration of pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: "Increased cultivation almost always produces a fastidiousness which renders necessary the increased elaboration of our pleasures... The superiority of a highly civilised man lies chiefly in the fact that he belongs to a higher order of being, for he has approached more nearly to the end of his existence, and has called into action a larger number of his capacities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast child/peasant (delight in simple objects) with cultivated persons who seek more elaborate, refined pleasures; civilised life may not yield more realised enjoyment but produces 'higher' ends and capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental pleasures valued despite lesser contribution to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: "...the vast and indisputable superiority which the general voice of mankind gives to mental pleasures, considered as pleasures, over physical ones... The former... are more varied and more prolonged than the latter but on the other hand, they are attained with more effort, and they are diffused over a far narrower circle."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes bodily conditions often have stronger effect on happiness (health, temperament); yet mental pleasures are ranked higher by common judgment. Example: inventor of anaesthetic may have improved happiness more than moral philosophers, but mental pleasures are still afforded higher status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral pleasures (gratification of moral feelings) are foremost
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a class of pleasures resulting from the gratification of our moral feelings which we naturally place in the foremost rank... no multiple of the pleasure of eating pastry can be an equivalent to the pleasure derived from a generous action."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or benevolent actions have a qualitatively higher worth even if not more intense; this supports hierarchy of pleasures and explains moral choices that prioritize worthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative distinctions challenge pure utilitarian accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: "This distinction of kind has been neglected or denied by most utilitarian writers... Consistently with that philosophy, the terms higher and lower... can have no other meaning than that of productive of more or less enjoyment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If qualitative distinctions exist, then choosing a pleasure for its 'worth' despite lesser enjoyment is inexplicable by simple greatest-happiness calculus; thus utilitarianism is inadequate to account for hierarchical valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Some moral differences arise from intellectual or empirical error
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are many cases in which diversities of moral judgment arise from causes that are not moral, but purely intellectual... the root of the condemnation of usury was simply an error in political economy... The question of the criminality of abortion has been considerably affected by physiological speculations as to the time when the fœtus... acquires the nature... of a separate being."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing divergent moral judgments, investigate factual, scientific, or economic misunderstandings (e.g., views about money, fetal animation) that underlie moral disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish duties of conscience from duties based on positive commands
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is a broad distinction to be drawn between duties which rest immediately on the dictates of conscience, and those which are based upon positive commands... The iniquity of theft, murder, falsehood, or adultery rests upon grounds generically distinct from those on which men pronounce it to be sinful to eat meat on Friday..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating moral injunctions, determine whether they are expressions of conscience (intrinsic moral duties) or derived from contingent religious/positive commands; their historical variability differs accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiquity and habit can transform means into sacred ends (customs become moral taboos)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Closely connected with the preceding are the diversities which result from an ancient custom becoming at last, through its very antiquity, or through the confusion of means with ends, an object of religious reverence... its violation was spoken of as a monstrous crime."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Roman prohibition on women tasting wine—initially pragmatic, later sacralised by habit and education. Analysts should trace whether reverence for tradition has obscured the original instrumental rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confused associations and popular perceptions can produce moral paradoxes
rubrics_metrics.description: "A confused association of ideas, which is easily exposed by a patient analysis, lies at the root of more serious anomalies... to contrast the admiration... excited by a conqueror... with the abhorrence produced by a single act of murder..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: admiration of conquerors despite atrocities — heroic self-sacrifice and national success can sanctify leaders; investigators should look for conflation of collective sacrifice with the moral character of prominent individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dogma and organised religion can override or pervert moral perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Another form of moral paradox is derived from the fact that positive religions may override our moral perceptions in such a manner, that we may consciously admit a moral contradiction... The contradiction is clearly perceived, but it is accepted by faith as part of the teaching of the Church."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances: transubstantiation, doctrines of damnation of unbaptised infants or reprobation—people accept moral contradictions because of authority, faith, or habit. When analysing moral beliefs, account for doctrinal pressures that suppress or invert intuitive moral judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dogmatic beliefs can justify extreme punitive practices
rubrics_metrics.description: "When therefore theologians believed that a man was intensely guilty who held certain opinions, and that he was causing the damnation of his fellows if he propagated them, there was no moral difficulty in concluding that the heretic should be put to death."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where theological or dogmatic systems teach grave metaphysical harms from opinions, moral reasoning about punishment may follow logically from those premises; analysts should expose the doctrinal premises that sanction persecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad intellectual education and inculcated credulity pervert moral faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: "When, for example, theologians during a long period have inculcated habits of credulity, rather than habits of enquiry... they will at last succeed in forming habits of mind that will instinctively and habitually recoil from all impartiality and intellectual honesty."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education that discourages inquiry and fosters habit can erode moral perception (as it does aesthetic and physical perception). Evaluations of moral standards should consider pedagogical and institutional formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral intuitionism: duty distinct from pleasure; intuitive hierarchy of affections
rubrics_metrics.description: "All that is necessarily meant by the adherents of this school is comprised in two propositions. The first is that our will is not governed exclusively by the law of pleasure and pain, but also by the law of duty... The second is that the basis of our conception of duty is an intuitive perception that... there are some [affections] which are essentially good... and some which are essentially bad."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author lists intuitively perceived hierarchies: benevolent affections superior to selfish ones; truth to falsehood; justice to injustice; gratitude to ingratitude; chastity to sensuality. Use these as baseline criteria when attributing an innate moral faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral unity is a unity of tendency, not uniform application of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: "Now it is manifest that according to this theory the moral unity to be expected in different ages is not a unity of standard, or of acts, but a unity of tendency... The question of morals must always be a question of proportion or of degree."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains cultural variation: same underlying direction (expansion of benevolence) manifests in different specific rules across stages (family → class → nation → humanity). When comparing societies, look for shared tendencies rather than identical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral progress compatible with innate moral perceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: "At this point, I may observe how completely fallacious is the assertion that a progressive morality is impossible upon the supposition of an original moral faculty... he fully admits that the degree in which they are acted upon... may become progressively higher."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two answers: (1) intuitive moralist allows standards to rise in degree; (2) acknowledgement that benevolence is a virtue means new knowledge about human interests can inform duties. Use this to reconcile intuitionism with historical moral progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual morals judged by degree of restraint and sanctity rather than identical prescriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The considerations I have urged with reference to humanity, apply with equal force to the various relations of the sexes... their object will be to abridge and confine the empire of sensuality... In these cases there is a great difference between the degrees of earnestness with which men exert themselves in the repression of their passions... but there is no difference in the direction of the virtuous impulse."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Jewish law, Greek, Roman, Catholic) show variable institutions (polygamy, monogamy, chastity, celibacy) yet a shared tendency to restrain sensuality and elevate sexual purity. When assessing sexual moral codes, consider degree, limits (e.g., necessity of species continuation), and the underlying tendency toward higher sentiment.
